description: Results-driven data team, transforming complex data into actionable insights.
summary: The Mediterranean Sea Climate Observatory (https://ahmed-madeh-noah.github.io/mediterranean-climate-observatory/) is an interactive web platform designed to investigate long-term environmental changes across the Mediterranean basin. Combining satellite observations and climate reconstructions from NASA GPM IMERG, Copernicus Marine, and KNMI Climate Explorer, the application examines nine key Earth system records spanning 1870 to 2025: sea surface temperature (SST), sea-level anomaly, ocean heat content (0–400 m), surface salinity, chlorophyll-a concentration, and coastal precipitation at Alexandria, Athens, and Barcelona.   Addressing the “Be An Earth System Trend Detective!” challenge, our tool empowers users to select locations, variables, and custom time windows to test whether observed changes are statistically significant or merely short-term noise. Using a custom in-browser statistical engine, it cross-examines trends across four parametric and non-parametric tests—including Newey–West (HAC) regressions and memory-corrected Mann–Kendall tests. By pairing interactive visualization with strict scientific guardrails, the platform helps researchers, students, and coastal planners distinguish true climate signals from natural variability in one of Earth’s fastest-warming seas.
details:
The Mediterranean Sea Climate Observatory (https://ahmed-madeh-noah.github.io/mediterranean-climate-observatory/) is a client-side analytical web application that turns users into climate trend detectives. Rather than showing static charts, it embeds curated multi-decadal time series from NASA, Copernicus Marine, and KNMI Climate Explorer alongside a custom-built JavaScript statistical engine (Stats and Adv modules) that computes live hypothesis tests in the browser. The platform is organized into eight interactive workspaces: Overview: Standardizes four headline variables (SST, Sea Level, Chlorophyll-a, and Alexandria Precipitation) into dimensionless z-scores (standard deviations) on a unified timeline so users can compare trend shapes across different physical units. Data Detective: A 6-step guided workbench where users select a location, pick a variable, adjust the start and end years via dual range sliders, and click "Watch the trend appear"—an animation that expands the time window year-by-year to demonstrate how sample size controls confidence intervals and p-values. Rain Compare: Compares NASA GPM IMERG half-hourly precipitation summed into annual totals (2001–2024) across three distinct Mediterranean climate regimes: Alexandria (31.25°N, 29.95°E), Athens (38.05°N, 23.65°E), and Barcelona (41.45°N, 2.15°E). Seasonality: Contrasts the Mediterranean's winter phytoplankton bloom (February peak at 0.122 mg m⁻³) and summer stratification desert (August minimum at 0.043 mg m⁻³) against monthly rainfall depth and peak half-hourly rain rates (mm/h). Variables, Region Map, Statistics, & Guardrails: Provides plain-language definitions, an interactive SVG map comparing the KNMI bounding box (30.19–45.98°N, 6.00°W–36.29°E) against the Copernicus sea mask and NASA 0.1° grid cells, full statistical tables, and methodological guardrails.

Key Scientific Findings:

Accelerating Surface & Subsurface Warming: Basin-wide satellite SST (NOAA OI v2, 1982–2025) is rising at +0.376 °C per decade (p < 10⁻¹⁵), roughly 6 times faster than the 1870–2025 background rate in HadISST1 (+0.064 °C per decade). Upper-ocean heat content (0–400 m, UKMO EN4, 1950–2025) rose by +0.234 × 10⁹ J/m² per decade (p = 0.000039). Rising Sea Levels: Satellite altimetry (1993–2021) confirms a steady basin-wide rise of +25.18 mm per decade (95% HAC CI: 19.61 to 30.74 mm/decade, p < 10⁻¹⁵), driven by thermal expansion and added water mass. Declining Primary Productivity (SDG 14): Basin-averaged surface chlorophyll-a (1998–2024) fell significantly by −0.0039 mg m⁻³ per decade (HAC p = 0.00054, Mann–Kendall tau = −0.41, p = 0.0031), reflecting stronger thermal stratification that blocks deep-water nutrients from reaching the sunlit surface. Opposing & Uncertain Coastal Rain Trends: Between 2001 and 2024, Alexandria precipitation sloped upward at +44.7 mm per decade (driven by extreme storm years in 2015 and 2020), while Athens (−38.3 mm per decade, p = 0.267) and Barcelona (−41.5 mm per decade, p = 0.445) sloped downward. Alexandria passes a standalone HAC t-test (p = 0.037), but fails the outlier-resistant Mann–Kendall test (p = 0.107) and fails false-discovery rate control when tested alongside Athens and Barcelona (q = 0.111).

Benefits & Intended Impact:

Standard trend calculators often mislead users by relying solely on Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) t-tests, which overstate certainty when climate records have strong year-to-year memory (autocorrelation) or extreme storm outliers. Our observatory solves this by scoring every selected time window across four simultaneous tests: OLS Student's t-test, Newey–West (HAC) autocorrelation-robust regression, non-parametric Mann–Kendall rank test with Theil–Sen median slope, and Hamed–Rao variance-corrected Mann–Kendall test. It also runs Pettitt change-point detection, continuous two-slope (hinge) regression, quadratic acceleration tests, sliding-window slope stability, and Benjamini–Hochberg (q-value) false-discovery adjustments. This supports UN Sustainable Development Goal 14 (Life Below Water) while teaching rigorous statistical literacy.

Tools, Coding Languages, & Software Used:

Built as a fast, zero-build single-page application using HTML5, CSS3 (custom dark/light Solaris theme with CSS Grid), and Vanilla ES6 JavaScript. Visualizations use Plotly.js (v2.35.2) alongside custom inline SVG sparklines, confidence-interval strips, and cartographic projections. All statistical distributions, regressions, and CSV exports run client-side in JavaScript.

Creativity & Factors Considered:

Instead of just telling users that short climate records are noisy, our "Watch the trend appear" simulation lets them experience how satellite SST from 1982 to 1998 appears statistically flat before emerging as an unmistakable warming signal over longer windows. We also built a dedicated "Scientific Guardrails" module explaining why a 0.1° land rainfall cell cannot be directly blamed for basin-wide ocean chlorophyll changes without watershed modeling, why bounding boxes differ from sea masks, and why ocean color is an optical proxy rather than a direct fish count.
